title: Inflation Fears Surge: Fed Survey Shows One-Year Outlook Highest Since May 2023【CNBC】
body:
Consumers’ expectations for price growth are climbing again, with the New York Federal Reserve’s latest Survey of Consumer Expectations showing the median 12‑month inflation forecast rising to 3.9 percent in September. The figure marks the highest near‑term outlook recorded since May 2023 and signals a resurgence of inflation worries that could shape monetary policy discussions in the months ahead.

The uptick arrives against a backdrop of mixed economic data. While the labor market remains robust, with unemployment holding steady at historically low levels, recent reports of slowing retail sales and a modest pullback in housing activity suggest that the economy is beginning to feel the strain of higher borrowing costs. The Federal Reserve has kept its policy rate in the 5.25‑5.50 percent range since July, aiming to curb price pressures without triggering a recession. Yet the new consumer sentiment data hints that households are beginning to anticipate a longer period of elevated prices, potentially eroding purchasing power and dampening discretionary spending.

Economists point to several factors that may be feeding the heightened expectations. Energy prices, which have risen modestly over the past month, continue to weigh on overall cost calculations, especially in regions still recovering from supply disruptions. Meanwhile, recent increases in food and rent prices have been felt directly by households, reinforcing the perception that inflation is not yet under control. “When people see their grocery bills and rent checks go up, it quickly translates into higher inflation expectations,” said Laura Chen, a senior economist at the Brookfield Institute. “Those expectations can become self‑fulfilling if they influence wage negotiations and price setting.”

The survey’s methodology, which gathers responses from a rotating panel of roughly 1,200 adults, offers a forward‑looking gauge that often precedes actual inflation readings. Historically, when consumer inflation expectations have risen sharply, the Fed has responded by tightening policy more aggressively. In the current cycle, however, policymakers appear to be walking a tighter rope. Some members of the Federal Open Market Committee have warned that premature rate cuts could reignite price pressures, while others argue that the economy’s resilience may allow for a more measured approach. The divergence within the Committee underscores the delicate balance between curbing inflation and preserving growth.

Market participants are already factoring the survey’s implications into pricing and investment decisions. Treasury yields have edged higher in recent sessions, reflecting expectations of a more hawkish stance, while equity markets have shown mixed reactions, with consumer‑focused stocks experiencing modest sell‑offs. Analysts caution that if inflation expectations continue to climb, the cost of borrowing could rise further, tightening credit conditions for both businesses and households.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of consumer inflation expectations will be closely watched as a barometer of economic sentiment. The Fed’s next policy meeting, slated for early December, will likely reference the survey’s findings alongside core inflation data that have recently hovered near the central bank’s 2 percent target. If the 3.9 percent outlook persists or rises, policymakers may feel compelled to maintain or even increase rates, prolonging the period of tighter monetary conditions. Conversely, a reversal in expectations could provide the leeway needed to begin easing policy later in the year. In either scenario, the evolving sentiment among consumers will remain a pivotal factor in shaping the United States’ inflation trajectory and the broader economic outlook.
